articles.title: Automatic abortion pardons clear women’s records in England and Wales
articles.summary:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Women in England and Wales who were arrested, cautioned or convicted for ending their own pregnancies no longer carry those records. Automatic abortion pardons took effect on November 16, and police and courts must now delete the details of past convictions, cautions, arrests and investigations wherever they can. The […]
The post Automatic abortion pardons clear women’s records in England and Wales first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News.
articles.content:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM

Women in England and Wales who were arrested, cautioned or convicted for ending their own pregnancies no longer carry those records. Automatic abortion pardons took effect on November 16, and police and courts must now delete the details of past convictions, cautions, arrests and investigations wherever they can. The women affected don’t need to apply, pay a fee, or contact anyone.

The pardons come under Section 242 of the Crime and Policing Act 2026, passed earlier this year alongside a separate provision that removed women from criminal law for ending their own pregnancies. Labour MP Tonia Antoniazzi, who brought forward the decriminalization amendment, says the change will clear the names of more than 100 women who were “unnecessarily harmed” by an “outdated” law.

How the abortion pardons work

Records deleted, or treated as deleted

The pardon applies to abortion offenses relating to a woman’s own pregnancy, including cases where she acted beyond the legal time limits. Where full deletion from police and court systems isn’t possible, records must be marked so they are treated as erased.

Alex Davies-Jones, the minister for victims and tackling violence against women and girls, said the pardons had been a priority. “Women do not have to take any direct action themselves, but can find out more information online and contact our dedicated casework team,” she said.

What remains illegal

The change ends prosecution of women over their own pregnancies, but abortion itself is still regulated. In England and Wales, abortion with an authorized provider is legal up to 24 weeks, with narrow exceptions after that point, such as when the mother’s life is at risk or the baby would be born with a severe disability. Medication taken at home is permitted before 10 weeks. Doctors and anyone else who act outside the Abortion Act 1967 can still face charges.

Ending a Victorian law’s reach

Nicola Packer’s five-year ordeal

The law that the change dismantles dates to 1861, and the cases brought under it in recent years show what it meant in practice. In 2020, during a Covid lockdown, Nicola Packer, then 41, was prescribed abortion medication by phone through the National Health Service. She believed she was a few weeks pregnant. In fact, she was around 26 weeks along.

Her friend Helle Tumbridge, speaking to the BBC with Packer’s consent, said she had experienced what’s known as a cryptic pregnancy. “That’s when you don’t have any sign of a pregnancy, no baby bump, no other symptoms,” she said. After a stillbirth, Packer went to the hospital, and staff called the police. “She was arrested. She spent a time in her hospital room recovering with two police officers present, one was a man. She was treated appallingly,” Tumbridge said.

It took five years of investigation before a jury unanimously cleared her. “Of course, by that point the damage had been done, and she’ll live with that trauma for the rest of her life,” Tumbridge said. The Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists said at the time that her trial showed “just how outdated and harmful” the law was.

Reactions to the pardons

Providers and advocates

Heidi Stewart of the abortion care provider BPAS acknowledged that a pardon has limits. “While no pardon can undo the distress and trauma these women have experienced, this historic change in the law recognises the profound harm caused by their criminalisation and represents a meaningful step towards justice,” she said.

Opponents of decriminalization

Not everyone sees the change that way. Anti-abortion groups opposed both decriminalization and the pardons, arguing that removing criminal penalties, including for abortions late in pregnancy, leaves the unborn without legal protection. John Deighan, CEO of the Society for the Protection of Unborn Children, said in April that the pardons law “disgraces the children who have been needlessly destroyed in the past.”

For the women whose records are now being cleared, the practical effect will show up in background checks, job applications, and travel paperwork that no longer carry a conviction or arrest. Antoniazzi and other supporters will be watching how smoothly police and courts carry out the deletions in the months ahead, since the pardon only works if the paperwork follows.

articles.title: Pip assessments need 'fundamental overhaul', report to say
articles.summary: Disability Minister Sir Stephen Timms says he will recommend major reforms to the personal independence payment.
articles.content:
A review into the personal independence payment (Pip) will call for a "fundamental overhaul" of the assessment process to "better recognise people's varying costs and needs", the disability minister has said.

Sir Stephen Timms has been looking into disability benefits in England and Wales for the past year and found the set up was "no longer fit for purpose".

Writing in the Times, external, he said his review, to be published on Tuesday, would recommend people with the most severe conditions have a "fast track" process which is "less burdensome".

It comes after a separate review into young people not in education, employment or training (Neets) recommended Pip be scrapped and replaced for under-25s.

Sir Stephen, who produced his report alongside disability groups, carers, clinicians and MPs, said that while Pip had the "right aims" when it was created, there have been "marked shifts in the nature of disability and ill health" in the 13 years since.

He said there had been "substantial growth in claims for mental health and neurodiverse conditions as well as changes to wider society and the workplace".

"For those with the most severe conditions and end of life care, the review recommends a fast track which is less burdensome, with assessment capacity freed up for other cases.

"Where claimants do not have additional costs or care needs, we should be signposting them to services and support."

He added: "Someone with a lifelong or degenerative illness should not need regular reassessments which feel adversarial and unnecessary.

"Disabled people must have the chance to participate fully in everyday life, including in work, and need a more personalised, flexible system that supports them to do so, rather than itself being a barrier."

The Timms review was commissioned after a U-turn from former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer's government on a plan for major benefit reform in an attempt to reduce the welfare bill by £5bn a year.

More than 130 MPs, including 120 from Labour, signed an amendment to reject plans to cut disability and sickness-related benefit payments in 2025.

The rebels said they opposed the plans because of the number of people expected to be pushed into relative poverty and a lack of consultation at the time.
articles.reasoning: The article reports on a government-commissioned review recommending a fundamental overhaul of the Personal Independence Payment (PIP) assessment process to better support disabled people, including a less burdensome fast track for severe cases and more personalized, flexible support. This has broad societal significance as it aims to improve the welfare system for disabled individuals, addressing systemic issues and promoting inclusion and dignity.

articles.title: Archaeologists reveal a powerful Iron Age king may have been a woman
articles.summary: Archaeologists have uncovered evidence that Verica, the Iron Age ruler whose exile helped trigger Rome’s invasion of Britain in AD 43, was actually a woman. The discovery challenges centuries of historical assumptions and suggests that a largely forgotten female leader may have changed the course of British history.
articles.content:
New archaeological research from Bournemouth University (BU) suggests that an influential Iron Age British ruler, long believed to have been a man, was actually a woman. The ruler, known as Verica, played a pivotal role in events leading to the Roman invasion of Britain in AD 43. The findings challenge longstanding assumptions about early British history and the political influence of women during this period.

Verica ruled the Atrebates, a powerful tribe whose lands extended across much of what is now Hampshire and West Sussex. Around AD 40, Verica was forced from power and escaped to Rome, where the exiled ruler sought assistance from Emperor Claudius.

The Roman historian Cassius Dio claimed that Verica's appeal was the reason Claudius decided to invade Britain. If this account is accurate, Verica's actions may have helped set in motion one of the most consequential events in British history.

Ancient Evidence Challenges an Iron Age King's Identity

Dr. Miles Russell, Director of Archaeological Fieldwork at Bournemouth University, led the research and argues that earlier historians incorrectly identified Verica as male.

"Verica is assumed to have been male because of the patriarchal mindset of 19th-century classical historians. Verica was not only critical to the special relationship between Britain and Rome in the early first century AD but was indisputably female."

Russell points to several pieces of evidence supporting this interpretation. One is the name Verica itself, which ends in the letter "a," a feature common among female names of the time. Other prominent examples include Cartimandua, who ruled the Brigantes (in Yorkshire), and Boudica, leader of the Iceni (in Norfolk).

All three rulers lived during roughly the same period. Boudica is the best known because of her rebellion against Roman rule in AD 60. However, Russell argues that Verica may have held even greater political power and influence.

Another important clue comes from coins issued under Verica's rule. These coins bear the Latin title "rex," traditionally translated as "king," which has contributed to the assumption that Verica was male. Russell explains that the title was not necessarily restricted to men.

"People also assume she was a 'he' because of the term 'rex' on coins, but rex is a non-gender-specific title; both male and female kings were recognized by Rome, Cleopatra of Egypt being the most famous."

He continued: "The use of the Latin title rex on coins shows that Verica ruled with the full authorization of the emperor."

The artwork on Verica's coins provides another intriguing clue. Rather than depicting the masculine warriors commonly featured on coins produced by other British Iron Age rulers, Verica's coins show a figure with distinctly feminine characteristics.

"Whilst other coin-producing British Iron Age leaders portray obviously male warriors, Verica is depicted as a slender, feminine, bare-breasted figure riding on horseback."

The Forgotten Ruler Behind Rome's Invasion of Britain

Russell believes Verica's importance extended far beyond the ruler's identity. He argues that Verica may have been instrumental in helping Claudius successfully invade Britain.

Ancient Roman writers frequently portrayed Claudius as an ineffective emperor who was easily influenced by women and formerly enslaved people who had gained their freedom. This reputation may have shaped how historians described Verica's role in persuading him to invade.

Russell suggests that Cassius Dio's account reinforced this negative portrayal by presenting the invasion as a decision made under the influence of a woman. In reality, he argues, Verica may have been a valuable political and military ally who supplied the Romans with intelligence and practical assistance.

"The story of Claudius committing to something only because a woman told him to fits the trope of this emperor as being submissive and henpecked. In effect, Dio was saying that the campaign was undertaken solely because of the whisperings of a barbarian femme fatale. Verica's role was rather more central to the British expedition. Having her on board ensured the project was a success, as she provided tactical information and support on the ground.

"The invasion was Claudius' great triumph -- it being the only chance he had to prove he was a successful military leader. Verica provided the excuse for regime change, and the emperor seized it."

For Claudius, the conquest of Britain offered an opportunity to establish his reputation as a successful military commander. Verica's removal from power gave him a political justification for intervening, while the exiled ruler's knowledge of Britain may have helped the Roman forces achieve their objectives.

Could Rome's Conquest of Britain Have Been Avoided?

Although Verica was an important political figure in late Iron Age Britain, the ruler's influence has received relatively little attention compared with that of other prominent leaders.

Russell believes the archaeological evidence supports recognizing Verica as one of Britain's earliest and most significant female rulers. He also raises the possibility that the Roman invasion might never have occurred without Verica's exile and subsequent appeal to Claudius.

"We should take the archaeological evidence at face value" says Russell "and remember Verica as a female-king and one of the earliest and most important of British female leaders. Had she not been deposed, fleeing to Claudius for military support, Rome may never have invaded Britain in the first place."

New Insights Into Women in Iron Age Britain

The findings build on earlier Bournemouth University research exploring the position of women in ancient British society.

Last year, a study involving Russell and other BU researchers uncovered evidence of a matriarchal society in Iron Age Britain. The research indicated that husbands moved into their wives' communities after marriage, suggesting that women occupied a central position in the social structure.

Together, these discoveries are prompting researchers to reconsider the influence women may have exercised in Iron Age Britain, both within their communities and in the political decisions that shaped the region's future.

Russell's research on Verica is presented in the new book Caratacus: Great king of Britain, published by Bloomsbury in January (ISBN 9781350477902). The findings are also discussed in the latest edition of Current Archaeology.

This finding has broad cultural and historical significance, reshaping understanding of female leadership and influence in ancient Britain, and promoting recognition of women's roles in history. articles.personality_presentation_es:
